- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: I ran ~74,600 probes, including an exhaustive contiguous sweep of every integer port in `[-300, 66600]`. Part (a) is airtight; I found one prose-level defect in part (b) plus several silences I resolved.

counterexamples.predictedByRule: line4 = 0 (INVALID). The rule's exhaustive leading-byte claim states "the ONLY bytes that keep the port parseable are 0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20 ..., '+' (0x2B) and '0'-'9'. Every other byte (including '-' which yields a negative, ...) gives line4 = 0." An implementer following that byte class rejects any '-'-led port substring.
counterexamples.actual: 1|1|1|1|0|  -> line4 = 1 (VALID). '-' IS consumed as a sign by the conversion, and "-0" yields the integer 0, which is a valid port. (The rule's grammar line "[+|-]?" and its Rust reference get this right; the byte-class prose contradicts them, so the rule is self-inconsistent and two implementers would disagree.)

counterexamples.predictedByRule: line4 = 0 per the byte-class prose ('-' is not in the parseable-prefix set)
counterexamples.actual: 1|1|1|1|0|  -> line4 = 1. Any '-' followed by whitespace-free all-zero digits (any length) gives port 0 => VALID.
1|1|1|1|0|  -> line4 = 1. Sign + zeros + ignored trailing junk => 0 => VALID. Same for "-0.5", "-0x10", "-0-0", "-0 ", " \t-0", and "http://h:-0/a/b" (1|1|1|1|2|a|b|).

1|1|1|0|0|  -> line4 = 0. CONFIRMS the rule: only the all-zero magnitude makes a '-'-led port valid, so the correct statement is 'the sign is parsed, and the resulting negative value is rejected by the range check' - not 'the byte is unparseable'.

input.correctedRule:
PORT: is_port_valid(int) + string->int port parsing  (corrected)

(a) is_port_valid(int p)  ==  (p >= 0 && p <= 65535)
    Now verified EXHAUSTIVELY, not by sampling: every integer p in [-300, 66600] was driven through the parser contiguously (66,901 runs) and line4 matched (0 <= p <= 65535) with ZERO anomalies. Additionally 4,156 wide probes covering the full int32 domain (all 2^k, 2^k+/-1, +/-(k*65536 + {-1,0,1,80,65535,65536}), int32 extremes 2147483647 / -2147483648 and neighbours, and 3,000 uniform random int32 values) all agreed. No holes, no second range, no clamping, no wraparound.
      0 -> valid; 65535 -> valid; 65536 -> invalid; every negative -> invalid.
    Rust: fn is_port_valid(p: i32) -> bool { (0..=65535).contains(&p) }

(b) How the int is produced.

Step 1 - locate the port substring (only inside an authority):
  - An authority exists only if the raw URL contains "://", located with find (FIRST occurrence, NOT rfind). Everything before it is the scheme (may be empty: "://:80" -> port 80 VALID; "://h:-0" -> 1|0|1|1|0). If "://" is absent, NO authority is parsed and port stays at the sentinel ("h:80" -> invalid; ":80" -> invalid; "http:h:80" -> invalid).
    * find, not rfind, proven via port: "http://a://h:80/x" -> 1|1|1|0|2|h:80|x| (authority is "a:", port_str is empty -> sentinel -> INVALID; rfind would have given port 80 VALID). Likewise "http://h:99999://a:80" -> line4 = 0 and "http://:80://h:99999" -> line4 = 1.
  - authority = text after "://" up to (but excluding) the FIRST occurrence of '/', '?' or '#', whichever comes first; else end of string. "http://h:80/a?b:99999" -> authority "h:80"; "http://h:8?0" -> port 8 valid; "http://h:8#0" -> port 8 valid; "http://h:6553?6" -> 6553 valid; "http://h:65535?0" -> 65535 valid; "http://h:6553/6" -> 6553 valid.
  - NEW (rule was silent): a '?' or '#' occurring BEFORE the "://" wins - the query/fragment is split off first, so the "://" inside it is never seen and no authority (hence no port) is parsed: "a?http://h:80" -> 1|0|0|0|1|a| (port INVALID); "a#http://h:80" -> same; "x?y://h:80/p" -> 1|0|0|0|1|x|; "http://a?b://h:80" -> 1|1|1|0|0| (port INVALID). A '/' before "://" does not prevent it: "http://a/b://h:80" -> 1|1|1|0|2|b:|h:80|.
  - If authority contains '@', split at the FIRST '@': userinfo = before, hostport = after.       let v = if neg { -acc } else { acc };
      if ovf || v > i32::MAX as i64 || v < i32::MIN as i64 { return -1; } // out_of_range
      v as i32
  }
  fn is_port_valid(p: i32) -> bool { (0..=65535).contains(&p) }

WHAT I COULD NOT BREAK - part (a) is in fact STRONGER than claimed. is_port_valid == (0 <= p <= 65535) survived an EXHAUSTIVE contiguous test of every integer in [-300, 66600] plus 4,156 samples spanning the whole int32 domain: zero anomalies. There is no hole, no second accepted window, no clamping, and no uint16/int32/int64 wraparound. I specifically hunted a wrapping accumulator with 2^32+80, 2*2^32+80, 2^31+80, 2^64+80, 2*2^64+80, 2^128+80 and the stoul-negation discriminators -4294967216 / -18446744069414584400; all INVALID, so the conversion really is i32 range-checked, matching std::stoi.

THE ONE REAL DEFECT (why 'corrected', not 'confirmed'): the rule is internally inconsistent about '-'. Its grammar line says [+|-]? and its Rust reference correctly returns 0 for "-0", but its prose asserts as an exhaustive byte-class fact that "the ONLY bytes that keep the port parseable are ... '+' (0x2B) and '0'-'9'. Every other byte (including '-' ...) gives line4 = 0." That is false: http://h:-0 gives line4 = 1. Anyone implementing from the byte class (rather than from the Rust) rejects '-' outright and diverges on the entire "-0" family. My two-byte sweep with prefix 0x2D nails the mechanism: of all 255 possible second bytes, ONLY '0' (0x30) produces line4 = 1 - conclusive proof that '-' is consumed as a sign and the resulting negative is then rejected by the [0,65535] check. In other words the rejection of negatives lives in is_port_valid, not in the grammar. That distinction is exactly the range-vs-sentinel boundary this lens is about.

SILENCES I RESOLVED AND FOLDED INTO THE CORRECTED RULE:
1. The "://" locator is find, not rfind, and it is observable through the port: http://a://h:80/x -> line4 = 0 (rfind would give 1); http://h:99999://a:80 -> 0; http://:80://h:99999 -> 1.
2. Order of operations: query/fragment splitting happens BEFORE authority extraction, so a '?' or '#' before the "://" destroys the authority (and the port) entirely: a?http://h:80 -> 1|0|0|0|1|a|; http://a?b://h:80 -> port invalid. A '/' before "://" does not.
3. Numeric base is definitively 10, not strtol base 0. Discriminators (absent from the original rule): :0177777 -> INVALID and :0x10000 -> VALID.
4. Sentinel: the weaker statement is PROVABLE, not just "natural" - since is_port_valid takes only an int and cannot see has_port, and no-port is false while 0 is true, the sentinel is provably outside [0,65535]. Exact value remains unobservable, as the engineer correctly said.
5. Robustness: a 100,000-digit port and 5,000-zero padding both parse without crashing (exit 0); the exception is caught locally in every out_of_range case I could construct.
6. Extra confirmations of the grammar's interaction with the range: appending a digit to 6553 or 65535 flips validity exactly as the value crosses 65535 ("6553<0-5>" valid, "6553<6-9>" invalid; "65535<any digit>" invalid), and '@' is the only trailing byte that ever invalidates a good port (it re-splits userinfo).

Untestable via argv, as the engineer noted: a 0x00 byte inside the port substring. Also genuinely indistinguishable and correctly flagged by them: std::stoi+try/catch vs strtol+errno vs a hand-rolled strtol with an explicit i32 range check - all three agree on every one of my ~74,600 probes, including all wrap and truncation discriminators.
